title: Many Ramayanas
hookLine: poets who loved Sita's story told her ending three different ways
carry: hari katha ananta: god's stories never end
tomorrow: was Rama right to send Sita away?
last: SITA IS A GODDESS, NAMED BEFORE RAMA.

lines: TELL IT, CHANGE IT, OR STOP?
cards: A poet sits with a pen in the air. The poet loves this story, knows it by heart, and is retelling it for a new audience, in a new language, long after Valmiki. Now the ending has come: Sita's exile, and the earth opening.
Tell it as it came down? Change it? Or quietly put the pen down before getting there?
Real poets faced exactly this choice, and they didn't all choose the same way.

teach.h: BHAVABHUTI: A PLAY WITH A REUNION.
teach.b: Start with Bhavabhuti, a Sanskrit playwright. His play is called the Uttararamacharita, the later story of Rama. He follows the exile closely and lets Rama's grief run deep.
But in the final act, Valmiki stages a play for Rama, a play about Sita, and when it ends, the earth goddess and the river Ganga bring Sita back, and husband and wife are reunited.
Bhavabhuti changed the ending, on purpose. Then there's Kamban, who sang the Ramayana in Tamil.
His great poem closes with Rama's crowning; it doesn't go on into the later book. And Tulsidas wrote the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi, a form of Hindi, still recited across North India.
His last section is also called the Uttar Kand, but it isn't a story of Sita's exile; it's mostly teaching and devotion. Keep the hard ending, rewrite it toward reunion, or end at the crowning.
None of these poets stands outside the faith looking in; the tradition treasures all three.
And Tulsidas gives the reason in his own poem: Hari is endless, and Hari's stories are endless, hari ananta, hari katha ananta, and the saints tell them and hear them in many ways.
Hindus don't keep one sealed Ramayana. They keep a living one, retold in Sanskrit and Tamil and Hindi and Bengali, on village stages and on television, and the retelling itself is devotion.
That's why a grandmother's Ramayana and a new picture book can differ, and both still be prayer.

how: Hindu communities meet the Ramayana through many retellings at once, Valmiki's Sanskrit, Kamban's Tamil, Tulsidas's Hindi and others, and families discuss Sita's exile openly, with different views at the same table.

games.q: a friend watched a cartoon Ramayana that ends with Rama and Sita together, and asks if that version is 'wrong'. by today's teaching, what fits?
o: retellings are old and loved; Bhavabhuti wrote a reunion too. Hari's stories are endless.
only Valmiki's counts; every other version is fake.
yes, changing a holy story is always forbidden.
games.why: Hindus keep a living Ramayana. Bhavabhuti, Kamban and Tulsidas each told it their way, and the tradition treasures them all.

practice: Choose one scene from the Ramayana you remember, any scene at all. Tell it to yourself silently, in your own words, as if to a child. That's katha, the way this story has always been passed on.
If you pray, end with Sita Ram. If you don't, end with one breath of thanks for whoever first told it to you.
